topic_tag: a printed ballad passed on by ear
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
blank_sentence: Comparing the versions, one folklorist concluded that a hundred years of singing had ______ the ballad.

worlds.passage: In 1790 a port-town printer sold a ballad about a young sailor who deserts his ship and drowns in a storm on his way home. A century later, folklorists collected it from singers who had learned it by ear. In nearly every version the storm still rises and the sailor is washed ashore alive, walking home to his mother's door. The verse in which his body is found appears in none of them, and the closing verse, which once cursed the sea, now describes his wedding. Comparing the versions, one folklorist concluded that a hundred years of singing had ______ the ballad.
worlds.explanation: The singers kept the story but softened its harshest parts, sparing the sailor and replacing the curse with a wedding, so singing had "mellowed" the ballad. "Moralized" fails because no lesson is drawn: the deserter is rewarded with a wedding rather than taught a consequence; "merged" fails because no other song is joined to it; "mangled" fails because the new version is a coherent story, not garbled.

moralized.why: a deserter who ends in a wedding draws no lesson; the punishment has simply been removed

merged.quote: walking home to his mother's door
merged.why: the change is to the ballad's own ending, not a joining with another song

mangled.why: the closing verse was deliberately rewritten, which is a coherent change, not damage

worlds.passage: In 1790 a port-town printer sold a ballad about a young sailor who deserts his ship and drowns in a storm on his way home. A century later, folklorists collected it from singers who had learned it by ear. In nearly every version the sailor still drowns, and the singers add a closing verse, found in no printed copy, addressed to "you young men who sign for the sea." Several singers told the collectors that it was the verse their fathers had made them learn before they first shipped out. Comparing the versions, one folklorist concluded that a hundred years of singing had ______ the ballad.
worlds.explanation: The singers kept the deserter's drowning and added a verse aimed at young sailors that fathers taught their sons before they went to sea, turning the story into a lesson, so singing had "moralized" the ballad. "Mellowed" fails because the sailor still drowns, nothing is softened; "merged" fails because the added verse speaks to this song's own subject and no other song is joined to it; "mangled" fails because the addition is clear and purposeful.

mellowed.why: the harsh ending is kept, so nothing has been softened

merged.quote: addressed to "you young men who sign for the sea."
merged.why: the new verse turns this ballad's story toward its listeners rather than bringing in another song

mangled.quote: made them learn before they first shipped out
mangled.why: the verse was understood and deliberately passed on, so the song was not garbled

worlds.passage: In 1790 a port-town printer sold a ballad about a young sailor who deserts his ship and drowns in a storm on his way home. A century later, folklorists collected it from singers who had learned it by ear. In nearly every version, once the storm rises, the song goes on with the verses of a farm girl's lament sold by the same printer, his name now set into its lines as her lost sweetheart's. The two songs share a tune and a rhyme scheme, and no singer could say where one ended. Comparing the versions, one folklorist concluded that a hundred years of singing had ______ the ballad.
worlds.explanation: The singers joined the ballad to a second printed song so smoothly that no one could find the seam, so singing had "merged" the ballad with another. "Mangled" fails because the joined song is seamless and makes sense, with the sailor's name fitted into the lament; "mellowed" fails because the sailor's fate is not softened: grief is added to it; "moralized" fails because the added verses mourn rather than teach a lesson.

mangled.quote: share a tune and a rhyme scheme
mangled.why: the two songs fit together cleanly, so the result is whole, not damaged

mellowed.why: adding a lament keeps the song sorrowful rather than softening it

moralized.why: the added verses express grief, not a lesson

worlds.passage: In 1790 a port-town printer sold a ballad about a young sailor who deserts his ship and drowns in a storm on his way home. A century later, folklorists collected it from singers who had learned it by ear. In nearly every version the topsail is now "the top of the hill," the home port is a name found on no map, and the sailor "weighs the anchor" by setting it on a scale. Asked what such lines meant, the singers shrugged and sang them again. Comparing the versions, one folklorist concluded that a hundred years of singing had ______ the ballad.
worlds.explanation: Words passed on by ear had turned into misheard phrases that no singer could explain, so singing had "mangled" the ballad. "Merged" fails because nothing from another song was joined to it; "mellowed" fails because the story is not softened, only garbled; "moralized" fails because the singers could not say what the lines meant, let alone draw a lesson from them.

merged.quote: a name found on no map
merged.why: the strange words come from mishearing, not from another song

mellowed.quote: by setting it on a scale
mellowed.why: the change is a garbled sense, not a gentler story

moralized.quote: the singers shrugged and sang them again
moralized.why: a lesson requires meaning, and the singers could not supply one
